{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=January 2019}}
{{Short description|Statistical parameter of random process evolution}}
In statistics, the '''residence time''' is the average amount of time it takes for a [[stochastic process|random process]] to reach a certain boundary value, usually a boundary far from the mean.

==Definition==
Suppose {{math|''y''(''t'')}} is a real, scalar [[stochastic process]] with initial value {{math|''y''(''t''<sub>0</sub>) {{=}} ''y''<sub>0</sub>}}, mean {{math|''y''<sub>avg</sub>}} and two critical values {{math|{''y''<sub>avg</sub> − ''y''<sub>min</sub>, ''y''<sub>avg</sub> + ''y''<sub>max</sub>}}}, where {{math|''y''<sub>min</sub> > 0}} and {{math|''y''<sub>max</sub> > 0}}. Define the first [[passage time]] of {{math|''y''(''t'')}} from within the [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] {{math|(−''y''<sub>min</sub>, ''y''<sub>max</sub>)}} as

:<math> \tau(y_0) = \inf\{t \ge t_0 : y(t) \in \{y_{\operatorname{avg}}-y_{\min},\ y_{\operatorname{avg}}+y_{\max}\} \},</math>

where "inf" is the [[infimum and supremum|infimum]]. This is the smallest time after the initial time {{math|''t''<sub>0</sub>}} that {{math|''y''(''t'')}} is equal to one of the critical values forming the boundary of the interval, assuming {{math|''y''<sub>0</sub>}} is within the interval.

Because {{math|''y''(''t'')}} proceeds randomly from its initial value to the boundary, {{math|τ(''y''<sub>0</sub>)}} is itself a [[random variable]]. The mean of {{math|τ(''y''<sub>0</sub>)}} is the '''residence time''',{{sfn|Meerkov|Runolfsson|1987|pp=1734–1735}}{{sfn|Richardson|Atkins|Kabamba|Girard|2014|p=2027}}
:<math> \bar{\tau}(y_0) = E[\tau(y_0)\mid y_0].</math>

For a [[Gaussian process]] and a boundary far from the mean, the residence time equals the inverse of the [[frequency of exceedance]] of the smaller critical value,{{sfn|Richardson|Atkins|Kabamba|Girard|2014|p=2027}}

:<math> \bar{\tau} = N^{-1}(\min(y_{\min},\ y_{\max})),</math>

where the frequency of exceedance {{mvar|N}} is
{{NumBlk|:|<math> N(y_{\max}) = N_0 e^{-y_{\max}^2/2\sigma_y^2},</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
{{math|σ<sub>''y''</sub><sup>2</sup>}} is the variance of the Gaussian distribution,
:<math> N_0 = \sqrt{\frac{\int_0^\infty{f^2 \Phi_y(f) \, df}}{\int_0^\infty{\Phi_y(f) \, df}}},</math>
and {{math|Φ<sub>''y''</sub>(''f'')}} is the [[power spectral density]] of the Gaussian distribution over a frequency {{mvar|f}}.

===Generalization to multiple dimensions===

Suppose that instead of being scalar, {{math|''y''(''t'')}} has dimension {{mvar|p}}, or <math>y(t) \isin \mathbb{R}^p</math>. Define a domain <math>\Psi \subset \mathbb{R}^p</math> that contains {{math|''y''<sub>avg</sub>}} and has a smooth boundary {{math|∂Ψ}}. In this case, define the first passage time of {{math|''y''(''t'')}} from within the domain {{math|Ψ}} as

:<math> \tau(y_0) = \inf\{t \ge t_0 : y(t) \in \partial \Psi \mid y_0 \in \Psi \}.</math>

In this case, this infimum is the smallest time at which {{math|''y''(''t'')}} is on the boundary of {{math|Ψ}} rather than being equal to one of two discrete values, assuming {{math|''y''<sub>0</sub>}} is within {{math|Ψ}}. The mean of this time is the '''residence time''',{{sfn|Meerkov|Runolfsson|1986|p=494}}{{sfn|Meerkov|Runolfsson|1987|p=1734}}

:<math> \bar{\tau}(y_0) = \operatorname{E}[\tau(y_0)\mid y_0].</math>

===Logarithmic residence time===

The logarithmic residence time is a [[dimensionless quantity|dimensionless]] variation of the residence time. It is proportional to the natural log of a normalized residence time. Noting the exponential in Equation {{EqNote|1}}, the '''logarithmic residence time''' of a Gaussian process is defined as{{sfn|Richardson|Atkins|Kabamba|Girard|2014|p=2028}}{{sfn|Meerkov|Runolfsson|1986|p=495|ps=, an alternate approach to defining the logarithmic residence time and computing {{math|''N''<sub>0</sub>}}}}

:<math>\hat{\mu} = \ln \left(N_0 \bar{\tau} \right) = \frac{\min(y_{\min},\ y_{\max})^2}{2 \sigma_y^2}.</math>

This is closely related to another dimensionless descriptor of this system, the number of standard deviations between the boundary and the mean, {{math|min(''y''<sub>min</sub>, ''y''<sub>max</sub>)/''σ''<sub>''y''</sub>}}.

In general, the normalization factor {{math|''N''<sub>0</sub>}} can be difficult or impossible to compute, so the dimensionless quantities can be more useful in applications.
